prompt: What does `@main` on `struct PlannerApp: App` do?
hint: A program has one of these.

choices.text: It makes the struct a class so SwiftUI can keep a reference to it
choices.why: It stays a struct; SwiftUI creates the value and reads its body.

choices.text: It marks the program's entry point
choices.why: Right: the `App` protocol supplies the `main()` the system calls at launch.

choices.text: It runs the body on a background thread
choices.why: An `App` is isolated to the main actor by default, the opposite.

choices.text: It lets several files each start the app
choices.why: Exactly one entry point is allowed among all the files.

prompt: Lesson 1's `week` ended when `main.swift` reached its last line. Why does `PlannerApp` not end when its `body` has been read?
hint: Who runs the app?

choices.text: Its body loops forever until the person closes it
choices.why: A body returns a description and nothing more; it contains no loop.

choices.text: iOS restarts it each time the body returns
choices.why: The process stays alive; nothing restarts it.

choices.text: SwiftUI owns the running program and keeps reading the description
choices.why: Right: the App is a value describing the app, and SwiftUI is what runs.

choices.text: The `@State` in it holds the process open
choices.why: State is data the views read; it does not decide how long a process lives.

prompt: On which actor do the properties and methods of `PlannerApp` run, unless you say otherwise?
hint: The protocol passes its isolation on.

choices.text: A new actor for each scene
choices.why: Scenes share the app's isolation; there is no actor per scene.

choices.text: Whatever thread called `main()`, with no isolation at all
choices.why: The documentation says a conforming type inherits `@MainActor` isolation.

choices.text: The main actor
choices.why: Right, the one that draws the screen, inherited from the `App` protocol.

choices.text: A background actor that the system picks
choices.why: Interface code wants the main actor, and that is the default here.

prompt: On an iPad, a person opens two planner windows from one `WindowGroup`. The plan is `@State` inside `CourseListView`. What happens when a session is added in one window?
hint: Read what the documentation says about storage per window.

choices.text: The other window does not show it, because each window has its own `@State`
choices.why: Right, which is why lesson 7 moves the plan into one model created in the App.

choices.text: Both windows show it, because they share one view
choices.why: A WindowGroup is a template: each window gets new views and new storage.

choices.text: The app crashes, since two windows cannot hold state
choices.why: Each window holds state perfectly well; it is just not shared.

choices.text: iPadOS closes the second window
choices.why: Nothing closes it; the two simply disagree.

prompt: What is a `WindowGroup`?
hint: It can make more than one window.

choices.text: The window the iPhone shows, created once
choices.why: On an iPhone it makes one window, but it is the template, not the window.

choices.text: A template for windows
choices.why: Right: its views are what each window it creates contains.

choices.text: A list of the app's views in the order they appear
choices.why: That is closer to a navigation stack, lesson 9.

choices.text: The macOS settings window
choices.why: That is the `Settings` scene.

prompt: Match each scene type to what it is for.
hint: One of them is the planner's.

pairs.right: Windows built from one template, as many as the platform allows
One window per file the app opens and saves

right_distractors: The phase a scene is in

prompt: A person goes to the home screen. Which phase does the planner's scene end up in?
hint: It is no longer visible.

choices.text: `inactive`
choices.why: Inactive is on the way; it is still in the foreground.

choices.text: `background`
choices.why: Right, and from there iOS may end the process.

choices.text: `active`, until the person closes it
choices.why: A scene that is not visible is not active.

choices.text: `suspended`, a fourth phase
choices.why: `ScenePhase` has three cases.

prompt: An iPad shows two planner windows; one is in front, the other is in the background. What does `scenePhase` read in the `App`, and in a view of the background window?
hint: Inside a view it is that view's scene; in the App it is an aggregate.

choices.text: `background` in both, since one window is hidden
choices.why: The App reports active if any scene is active.

choices.text: `active` in both, since the app is in front
choices.why: A view reads its own scene's phase, and its scene is in the background.

choices.text: `active` in the App, `background` in that view
choices.why: Right: the App aggregates, and a view reads its own scene.

choices.text: `inactive` in the App, because the two disagree
choices.why: There is no averaging; any active scene makes the App active.

prompt: Put the phases a scene passes through in order: active, then the person goes home and comes back.
hint: Four moves after the first active.

prompt: Why is a person closing an app not the moment to save its data on iOS?
hint: What usually happens instead of closing?

choices.text: Closing an app deletes its files first
choices.why: Files survive; the problem is that the moment rarely comes.

choices.text: People rarely close apps, and iOS ends some in the background without warning
choices.why: Right, so the app saves on leaving active, as Apple's documentation advises.

choices.text: SwiftUI forbids writing files after `onChange` runs
choices.why: Nothing forbids it; a short write in `onChange` is what section 07 does.

choices.text: A closed app keeps running, so there is no need
choices.why: An ended process runs nothing.

prompt: The first `Lifecycle` returned `.refresh` on every move to `.active`. Which test caught it?
hint: A move to active that never went through the background.

choices.text: `goingHomeSavesOnceAndComingBackRefreshes`
choices.why: That journey does go through the background, so refreshing there is right; it passed.

choices.text: `aBannerSavesAndDoesNotRefresh`
choices.why: Right: a banner returns to active without the background, and got `.refresh`.

choices.text: `mondayIsTheStartOfTheWeek`
choices.why: That is lesson 1's, and it passed both times.

choices.text: None: both lifecycle tests passed
choices.why: The first run failed with one issue.

prompt: A scene goes active → inactive → background → inactive → background → inactive → active (the person peeked at the app switcher twice). What does the second `Lifecycle` return for the final move?
hint: `wasInBackground` is set by any background and cleared only by active.

choices.text: `.nothing`, since it was inactive just before
choices.why: The flag remembers the background across the inactive moves.

choices.text: `.save`, since it passed through the background twice
choices.why: Save is for leaving active, not arriving.

choices.text: `.refresh`, once
choices.why: Right: the flag was set, so arriving at active refreshes and clears it.

choices.text: `.refresh` twice, one per background
choices.why: One move returns one action.

prompt: In `case (_, .active) where wasInBackground`, the part after `where` is a condition that a matching ___ must also satisfy.
hint: The thing a case of a switch is made of.

prompt: Why does `Lifecycle` use the planner's own `Phase` rather than SwiftUI's `ScenePhase`?
hint: Where were the tests run?

choices.text: `ScenePhase` has more cases than the planner needs
choices.why: It has the same three; `Phase` mirrors it case for case.

choices.text: So it compiles and is tested without SwiftUI, on Linux
choices.why: Right: nothing in the package imports SwiftUI.

choices.text: `ScenePhase` cannot be used in a `switch`
choices.why: Section 07 switches over it to build a `Phase`.

choices.text: Apple deprecated `ScenePhase` in iOS 17
choices.why: It is current, and the app reads it in section 07.

prompt: How many tests ran in each `swift test` of section 05?
hint: Two of lesson 1's and two new ones.

prompt: In SwiftUI, how does a tap in `SessionForm` reach the plan that `CourseListView` owns?
hint: Events travel up the tree in a particular form.

choices.text: The form repaints the list's rows itself
choices.why: Nothing in SwiftUI paints another view; you describe, SwiftUI draws.

choices.text: By calling a method on the parent view object
choices.why: Views are values the parent recreates; there is no object to call.

choices.text: As a change to data the parent owns, through a binding or a model
choices.why: Right: lesson 6 is the binding and lesson 7 the observable model.

choices.text: Through a notification the whole app listens to
choices.why: That would work around the tree rather than through it.

prompt: Why can `List(courses)` take the array of courses directly?
hint: Lesson 1 gave `Course` a conformance for this.

choices.text: Because `Course` is a struct
choices.why: Being a struct says nothing about identity.

choices.text: Because the array is a `let`
choices.why: A `var` would work as well.

choices.text: Because `Course` is `Identifiable`
choices.why: Right: each row is known by its course's `id`, lesson 8's subject.

choices.text: Because `List` sorts any array by title before showing it
choices.why: List shows the order it is given, and sorts nothing.

hint: Four screens, the same on every platform.

prompt: Which belongs in `@SceneStorage`?
hint: Something cheap to lose.

choices.text: The plan's courses and sessions, so nothing is lost
choices.why: SceneStorage is destroyed with its scene and has no timing guarantee; data goes to disk.

choices.text: Which course was open
choices.why: Right: small, per scene, and harmless if a window is removed.

choices.text: The person's password
choices.why: The documentation says not to use it with sensitive data.

choices.text: The week's total minutes, to avoid summing again
choices.why: The total is derived from the plan; lesson 6 computes it rather than storing it.

prompt: Why does `Phase.init(_:)` need `@unknown default` in its switch over `ScenePhase`?
hint: Whose enum is it?

choices.text: Because `ScenePhase` has a fourth case iOS 17 added
choices.why: It has three; the clause is for cases that may come.

choices.text: Apple's enum, free to gain cases later
choices.why: Right: the compiler asks for it on an enum from another module that is allowed to grow.

choices.text: Without it the switch would crash at run time
choices.why: The compiler warns before anything runs.

choices.text: To save the plan when the phase is unknown
choices.why: It maps an unknown phase to inactive, which does nothing.

prompt: Why is the planner's `onChange(of: scenePhase)` attached to the `App` and not to `CourseListView`?
hint: The plan is shared by every window.

choices.text: Views cannot read the environment
choices.why: Any view can read `scenePhase`; section 04 shows one.

choices.text: The App runs before every view, so it is faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: In the App the phase is the aggregate of every window, which fits a shared plan
choices.why: Right: a view would see only its own scene.

choices.text: `onChange` exists only on scenes
choices.why: It exists on views too.

prompt: A colleague proposes saving the plan only in `.background`, never in `.inactive`. With the second `Lifecycle` in mind, what is lost?
hint: What does Apple's documentation say about leaving the active state?

choices.text: Nothing, because every journey reaches the background
choices.why: A banner never reaches the background.

choices.text: The refresh, which then never happens
choices.why: Refreshing is decided on arriving at active, unaffected by when saving happens.

choices.text: The save at the moment Apple advises, leaving active
choices.why: Right: if the app is ended before reaching the background, the work typed since is gone.

choices.text: The tests, which can no longer run on Linux
choices.why: Either rule is plain Swift and tests the same way.
